newsitem.title: USA: Party leader predicts Gingrich re-election.
newsitem.headline: Party leader predicts Gingrich re-election.

text.p: Republican Party chairman Haley Barbour predicted Friday that Newt Gingrich will be re-elected House speaker with almost every Republican backing him even though he had admitted breaking House ethics rules.

During an interview with "Fox Morning News," Barbour dismissed a Friday report by the New York Times that 27 House Republicans are unwilling to commit themselves to voting for Gingrich as "the rankest sort of speculation."

Barbour's comments, a preview of a news conference by him later Friday, were the latest in an intensive campaign by Gingrich's allies to keep Republican troops in line against increasing Democratic criticism of Gingrich.

The House, controlled by Republicans 227 to 207 Democrats and one independent who usually votes with the Democrats, convenes Tuesday, when it is expected to elect its leaders, including House speaker -- the nation's highest elective post behind president and vice president.

"I believe Newt Gingrich will be re-elected speaker by a comfortable margin, that virtually every Republican will vote for him for a simple reason -- there's been nothing in the ethics process to disqualify him," Barbour said.

It would require 20 defections by Republicans for Gingrich to lose his job. The Georgia Republican is credited with spearheading the Republican drive to win control of the House in 1994 for the first time in 40 years.
Gingrich's troubles came to a head after a Dec. 21 report by a subcommittee of the House ethics committee that had been investigating allegations against Gingrich.
The House leader acknowledged providing false information to investigators and failing to ensure that he complied with laws barring use of tax-exempt contributions for partisan political purposes.
But Gingrich said he been "in some ways, naive" and had not intended to mislead the committee.

Republicans were said Thursday to be circulating reports the ethics investigative subcommittee had decided on a reprimand against Gingrich, a lesser punishment than a censure. A censure would seem certain to cost Gingrich his job.

But special counsel James Cole, a non-government criminal lawyer hired to investigate the Gingrich accusations , said in a statement: "There have been recent press reports concerning the work of the investigative subcommittee and any recommendation it might make. Those statements and reports are not accurate."
Party chairman Barbour, a close friend of Gingrich, said a reprimand would be the proper action from what he has read of the subcommittee report.
"This would be totally consistent with the findings that were publicly released," Barbour said of a reprimand.
He blamed Democrats for trying to drag out the Gingrich investigation.

"Here is an effort by the Democrats to pervert the ethics process, to try to win through that what they couldn't win at the ballot box," Barbour said of Democrats who lost last November an attempt to win back a majority in the House.
"This is a pure partisan power play," he said.

He compared the Gingrich case to an ethics committee investigation of House Democratic Leader Richard Gephardt who had been accused of not disclosing income from a beach front home in his financial statements. Last September the ethics committee dismissed the case once Gephardt resubmitted proper documents.
Barbour ridiculed the Gephardt case, saying that the committee merely said to him "Please don't do it again."
